item.title: Free Speech Is The Wrong Problem
item.description:
Everyone agrees that online platforms have a problem with free speech. They just can't agree on whether we need more of it or less of it.

But maybe Free Speech is the wrong way to think about the problems that online platforms have, and the real problem that speech needs to flow in better ways.

It’s tempting to think of free speech as being a dial that you can turn up or down. Turn it down to zero and you get the approved opinions of the Chinese Communist Party or BigCorp. Turn it up to 11 and everyone has a personalized feed of crazy, telling them to drink bleach and hate everyone. In this model, all you have to do is to find the right place to turn the dial.

Indeed for many kinds of content this “turn the dial” approach works pretty well. For sex and violence, platforms like Facebook (where I worked in the Integrity org) make a somewhat arbitrary decision about how sexy or violent something can be before it isn’t allowed, build unavoidably noisy systems to detect such content, and make a somewhat arbitrary decision about how to make the trade off between false positives (e.g. taking down innocent baby photos) and false negatives (e.g. keeping up active shooter videos). People complain a bit on the edges, but by and large it works remarkably well.

Where this approach doesn’t work well is controlling the spread of ideas. 

Let’s start with a fictitious example of how ideas can spread badly. 

Alice writes an article saying “Eating Cheese Prevents Leprosy”. She isn’t meaning to deceive people - she’s just really bad at statistics. She shares it with some of her pro-dairy friends who re-share it to show their loyalty to dairy. A few layers of shares later, the post is going viral, reshare-optimized ranking algorithms are putting it top of everyone’s feeds, and the dairy industry is using ads to boost distribution. Ad-funded news sites see that the topic is trending and quickly produce copycat articles, including some that say cheese makes you immortal, or immune to vampires. Millions of people, seeing similar arguments from many sources, assume it to be true, switch to cheese only diets, and get admitted to hospital with cheese overdoses.

A day later the original pro-cheese article reaches the anti-cheese community. The community only consists of 5 people, but they are very loud and each have a thousand fake accounts. They write posts arguing that eating cheese is a pro Darth Vader idea. A few online influencers, wanting to distance themselves from Darth Vader, join in the pile on. The Russians decide that Cheese is a good wedge issue to divide America and amplify the pile-on. Alice’s employer hadn't realized that eating cheese was now a taboo idea, but it seems everyone else thinks it’s, so they quickly fire Alice to avoid PR problems.

This isn’t a real example, but it’s very nearly a real example. This is pretty much how social media works, and it’s terrible.

So what went wrong here?

The problem wasn’t that Alice’s original article should have been blocked by her social media platform. Maybe eating cheese actually does prevent leprosy and further scrutiny would have confirmed that important discovery. Or maybe investigating the flawed cheese-leprosy connection would have revealed something valid.

The first thing that went wrong was that Alice’s original idea spread too fast, without waiting for it to be validated. The second problem was that, by putting it in everyone’s feeds, apparently from multiple sources, the platforms created a false consensus effect, that caused readers to think it was accepted truth. Essentially the same thing then happened for Alice’s firing, with the argument against her spreading too fast without scrutiny, creating a false consensus belief that she needed to be fired.

We also have a load of other problems that contribute to this mess. Journalists who are rewarded for saying things that are interesting rather than things that are right. Fake accounts and disproportionate engagement that make online behavior a poor proxy for what real people think. “Open and Connected” spaces that take away the ability for different groups to peacefully enforce internal cultural norms without fighting each other.

Really the whole thing is a mess and it’s amazing humanity hasn’t set itself on fire by now. But the problem isn’t free speech - it’s the way information flows between people.

So what might better speech flow look like? 

Maybe we we can get inspiration from in-person organizations. Inside a well-functioning in-person organization, problems are typically dealt with through nested groups and privacy. If Alice has a new idea, she starts by discussing it privately with someone she knows. If that goes well then she can present her (likely refined) idea to a small private group, or test it experimentally. If that goes well, then the ida gets presented to increasingly big groups as it gets increasingly validated.

And indeed organizations don’t have to be in-person to operate this way. Lots of remote organizations running on platforms like Slack distribute information in roughly this manner, with much less chaos than social media. What matters isn’t that these organizations are in-person, but that they have structure, gatekeepers, and hierarchy.

So maybe we have a second dial we can turn to choose how “structured” our information flow should be, similar to the “free speech” dial. It’s tempting to think that the “structure” and “free speech” dials are the same, but they are pretty different. You could have a very structured space with extreme free speech, where anyone can say whatever taboo idea they like in their small group, and those taboo ideas will flow up to the next level group if they get lower level support.

So maybe “social town square” platforms like Facebook and Twitter would benefit from having more of this kind of structure - from feeling more like a workplace?

Maybe they would. Except so far nobody has found a good way to make this work. Most people don’t want their personal social communication to feel like BigCorp, and if platform companies give people a product they don’t like then they will leave (unlike BigCorp, where management decides on your platform).

So what happens next?

Maybe someone comes up with a better product idea that changes the world (I’m working on some myself)? Maybe our culture adapts to be able to cope better with borderless communication? Maybe people retreat into the arms of structured organizations in order to more trustworthy information. But I do hope we move on from thinking we can solve this problem by turning the free speech dial.

item.title: An Attempt at Top-down Interpretability
item.description:
There are at least two distinct ways to conceptually organize a scientific endeavor: top-down or bottom-up. The bottom-up approach involves finding the smallest objects we can confidently understand, studying them, and leveraging that knowledge to study more complex objects made up of those smaller pieces. As a highly simplified example, in mech-interp this might mean starting by first understanding single neurons/SAE directions/features, leveraging this understanding to study circuits/manifolds composed of those neurons, and finally building a understanding of the model as a composition of circuits. By way of analogy, if our goal was restore a photo, the bottom-up approach starts by restoring the individual pixels, using this as a guide to restore patches, and finally to put it all together.

The top-down approach instead tries to get a coarse picture of the whole object, and uses those intuitions to understand motifs, and then zooms into mechanics of those motifs. For the mech-interp, this might involve getting some vague sense of what sort of information the model contains the what the model does with that information, studying the subspaces and broad phases that create and manage that information, and then finally study the mechanics of those pieces. Following the previous analogy, we start by getting a blurry version of the whole picture, and use this to identify the most important broad pieces to study, and finally extend the understanding the whole model.

This post contains some initial attempts on doing top-down interpretability. These are really just a lightly edited version of my own research notes, and are largely exploratory and preliminary. Most of these are conclusions drawn from a wide variety of particular experiments and tests-- if you have interest in any particular part I can add a comment where I write up the evidence in more detail.

The post is roughly organized around the following broad curiosity:
How is the residual stream organized? What does it contain? How is it used by the model?

As a final note before the main content: I study Gemma-4-31B-base here. I chose this model fairly arbitrarily, primarily motived by the belief that this model is sufficiently intelligent to be worth studying, the architecture is simple (there is no MoE), and I can run it locally. I have not done a meaningful comparison to other models, but a cursory look suggests the model's scape is far more anisotropic than others. This ended up being helpful, so I stuck with this model.

TL;DR: I looked at how the residual stream of Gemma-4-31B-base is organized, starting from its coarse shape. I find the residual stream highly anisotropic and shift a lot across layers in raw coordinates, but becomes more balanced and stable across layers when we read the stream through the pre-MLP RMSNorm. I study this 'corrected' space and find that the middle layers (~L20–L40) split into a few distinct parts. I zoom into one of them, a set of ~600 small and unusually stable coordinates that seems to function as a crucial reference for the model and the common source of most of its computations. Keeping only these coordinates (plus a handful of norm-controlling ones) at the final position nearly preserves the model’s predictions, while keeping the other ~90% breaks it. Patching experiments suggest this space holds the current token along with its contextual meaning (e.g. which sense of “bank” is meant). This is my first interpretability project and these are lightly edited research notes, so treat the conclusions as preliminary. I mainly wanted some technical practice to up skill into the field, and wanted to share the results in case they are useful for anyone else.


What is the Residual Stream's Shape?

I'll start with a few observations about Gemma-4-31B in particular. Gemma-4-31B uses a sandwich norm, which means the RMSNorm is applied both before an operation, and after.


Because the RMSNorm is applied both before and after either the Attention or MLP operation, the attention/mlp operations are somewhat buffered from need to 'internally' use the same scale as the residual stream. The model can, somewhat freely, retain its own internal coordinate scale while storing a different one in the residual stream.

The residual stream in Gemma-4-31B is, as a result, highly anisotropic. I averaged the residual stream over ~1024 passages (right before the MLP block) to produce this table.

which shows that the large coordinates (95% percentile) are about ~2 OOMs larger than the small coordinates (5% percentile).

The residual stream was really never meant to be measured in raw coordinates, and Gemma's extreme unevenness is nice illustration of this fact. The more 'natural' coordinates for the residual stream is the size after applying the RMSNorm. I'll shelve the term that comes from dividing the size of the residual stream for now, and focus just on the pre-MLP diagonal .

A reasonable first hypothesis is that is roughly equally sized in all directions, but only in its 'natural' coordinate system (As mentioned, we will shelve the term for now, and focus just on the diagonal). What would this mean? Assume a coordinate in the residual stream varies between and , and coordinate varies between and . If the model viewed these coordinates as equally sized, then the diagonal for should be , and the diagonal for should be . This way, in the 'natural' metric, both coordinates vary between and . If this is the case, coordinate that are naturally smaller in raw size within the residual are compensated by larger diagonal, and vice-versa for naturally larger coordinates.

We can test each coordinates 'natural variance' by computing the value of the residual stream across some examples and measuring the size of one standard deviation in that coordinate. At layer 20, this gives us the following (log-log) plot:

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the diagonal gain per coordinate is almost perfectly inversely proportional to the standard deviation across nearly all orders of magnitudes (i.e. ). That is, small coordinates really are read with a large diagonal to compensate for being small, and large coordinate are read with a small diagonal to compensate for being large.

Here are the values from fitting a line with slope (in log space) onto the various layers SD to diagonal relationship.

Thus, the first thing we learn is that the model seems to 'work' in a metric where the coordinate activations are roughly isotropic, even though the raw coordinates are not. The of the part of the RMSNorm is also quite stable and, at each layer, is roughly constant (for reason I'll address in the next section). I'll denote the median value of by (I've dropped the subscript of the layer for convenience, but does vary per layer). Since for each layer, this gives us what seems to be a reasonable norm to work in. So, from this point on, I'll largely not use raw residual stream coordinates as the norm-- instead it seems that when we measure we ought to first correct by multiplying .

Once we switch to this new coordinate system , the residual stream starts to look a lot more stable than it did before. Whereas before the residual stream varied over multiple orders of magnitude, is quite stable. We'll denote the residual stream after the diagonal mapping as (or for the ith coordinate), and write when we want to emphasize the layer.

Here is a plot of the residual stream, averaged over 128 passages, and then transformed into the new coordinate system. Each dot has as its x coordinate the size of one standard deviation in that coordinate and as its y coordinate the average value of (i.e. the coordinates are ), Despite coordinates varying over many orders of magnitude in size, the coordinates stay within a fairly narrow range in the new coordinate system.

For the sake of the next two graphs, I add one more constant parameter per layer to make the average height 1.

In this graph, I color the coordinates by how much, on average, they move between layers. This gives a sense of which coordinates are actively varying, and which are staying stable. More precisely, we color by.

There are various interesting patterns to track in this graph, which we will look at in more detail later. For instance, there seems to be a stable space at a small scale, a much more active space in the larger scale, and a surprising amount of stability between each update, and large transformations at various specific layers. As a final check, we can apply this to a random single token at a random sentence to check that we are stabilizing the scale on particular examples as well.


We see that the diagonal is normalizing the scale here, and about the same motifs as the averaged example (two distinct sizes, spaces that are stable, multiple phases of computation).

A few observations to follow and explore in the next section:

  • The residual stream has a anisotropic shape, but becomes isotropic once we look at the residual stream as the model uses it.
  • The residual stream appears to bifurcate into two main scales. Plotting on a linear scale, most of the coordinates bunch at once scale, with a smaller group clumping at a smaller scale. There is additionally a third, small group whose size is too large to fit into the graph.


What are the Parts and Phases of the Residual Stream?

The residual stream contains multiple distinct phases and parts. The majority of my interest and research has been in the middle phase, which I define as roughly starting at roughly L20, and ending at L40. I will say more on the phases later, but let us first look at study this middle region and identify its parts.

As mentioned in the last section, the residual stream bifurcates into two distinct main scales, with a third small clump of large coordinates. Let us first look at that third small clump.

Scale 1: Very large Coordinates

If we plot the entire natural variation versus norm gain, we find that there are a few noticeable outliers.

These coordinates have both very large size, and very low diagonal readout strength. That means these coordinates are large in the raw residual stream, but very small to the actual attention computation. That is, they contribute strongly to the norm computation, but not much to the actual MLP computation. The coordinate 2041 at layer 25 alone contributes ~ of the norm energy, but only ~ of the readout energy. Here is a plot of a few of the coordinates across the middle layers, and their norm contribution.

These coordinates contribute most of the norm size, but are read out with a very small size. Removing these tokens effect on the norm has a major impact on loss, whereas zeroing out there read does practically nothing.

I believe these norm control coordinates have been observed many times, so I will mainly comment on the importance for this post.

  • When we make interventions, we should leave the norm coordinates alone. For instance, when we zero, we should ensure we don't zero the norm coordinates. Zeroing the norm coordinates messes with the scale the model like to work in.
  • We must be especially careful in cases where we adjust for scale by inverting the diagonal . (For a case where we might do this: if we wanted to study the Jacobian matrix, then Gemma's unbalanced raw residual norm would make small coordinates unreasonably influential and large coordinates unreasonably ineffective (per unit norm change). Changing a coordinate that varies between and by appears to have a much larger effect, but this may only be because our perturbation is not in the right metric). Since these coordinates have such a small read strength, is huge in these coordinates. However, these coordinates have a small read strength for a separate reason then other coordinates do-- the model intends to ignore these coordinates in its computations. In most cases, I treat the norm coordinates separately than the rest, and just hold them out of most computations. The model seems to want to keep these directions roughly constant, and so I try to respect this preference in interventions and computations.

I will refer to these coordinates as the Norm coordinates. I conservatively pick out 53 of these coordinates that are outliers within the L20-L40 range, and so also refer to these as the Norm53 coordinates. Though just 3 coordinates is basically sufficient to capture all the norm energy.

Scale 2: Very Small Coordinates

Most of the remainder of this post will be focused on these nature of the small coordinates. There is a set of roughly ~600 coordinates that have a conspicuously smaller size than the rest of the coordinates between the layers L20-L40. I'll refer to these as the Quiet coordinates or Quiet600, since these coordinates are 'quiet' within the residual stream. It is worth noting that this is a bit of a misnomer though, since these are perhaps the most important coordinates within the residual stream.

First, let us get a birds eye view of 'activity' within each coordinate. We use the diagonal to suggest the natural 'size' of the coordinate, and color each coordinate by how large the writes to each coordinate are. For instance, the diagonal was , then the natural range of the coordinate is viewed to be to , and so a write of would account for of the coordinates range, so would be colored in the green-blue range. A write of would be of the implied size and be colored in the orange-red range. I've split the Quiet600 into two parts, the Persistent279, and the rest of the Quiet coordinates. There are a few other spaces I highlight as outliers, though I might not get to them until the next post. Also note that I follow the same coordinate across layers, so one row follows a single fixed coordinate from layer to layer .

There are at least a few important observations.

The large 'Other' set is nearly uniform, which is evidence that it is not coordinate aligned. If the space were not coordinate aligned, then a single coordinate is essentially a random probe into its state, so when we average over many examples every coordinate looks identical. Thus, the majority of the residual stream is not coordinate aligned.

The Quiet600 space stands out. This suggests these coordinates are a part of some subspace that is coordinate aligned. This doesn't imply the individual coordinates are meaningful, but that there is a distinctive subspace contained within those 600 coordinates.

The writes to Quiet600 are much smaller than the rest of the space. These writes are much smaller than the writes elsewhere.

The same set of coordinates remain distinctive throughout the middle phase. For the Quiet remain coordinates, they seem to remain stable from ~L20 to ~L35, whereas the 'Persistent' set remains stable until the start of ~L40. This means that this distinctive space is staying within within the same subspace.

There are a few other outlier groups (Late377, Late171), but the Quiet set apparently captures nearly all the coordinate aligned subspace.

This is enough reason to be interested in this space, let us now understand it.

How is the Quiet Space distinct?

The Quiet (and its subset the Persistent) space have a few properties that make then distinctive.

First, this space is highly stable. The stability of this space very high, but this fact can easily be obscured by measuring in raw coordinates. At each layer, there is a constant that multiplies the whole residual stream, so any stable space is forced to decay across layers. Indeed, this set of coordinates does undergo that decay in size, which you may have observed in the earlier gif as one set of coordinates seemed to move moving leftward.

Mathematically, across L20 - L40 any stable data ought to decay purely from the layer-wise scaling. Thus, the data in L40 ought to be about ~x smaller than it was at the start of L20. And indeed, the data in the 'Persistent' set does decay, we empirically see the median standard deviation decrease by x (that this is less than x suggest some small writes that are aligned with the current coordinates, and therefore slow the decay), while the median reader in these coordinates increases by ~x. In raw residual coordinates this space is undergoing a significant change in scale, but after adjusting for the MLP read the median reader is nearly constant in scale at ~x.

When we measure each layer's residual stream in the MLP coordinates , we find that the persistent set has a high cosine similarity between adjacent layers, and drifts only very gradually.

Should be view it as surprising that there are some coordinates that remain stable for many layers? Given that each layer does have a fully dense write, some coordinates should make it through a few blocks simply by chance. Heuristically, if we take the writes at each layer (and adjust to SD) and then redistribute those to random coordinates we can get a sense of how many coordinates should slip through on an example just by luck.

In general, many coordinates survive a few blocks simply because they haven't had time to be overwritten, but we expect less than one to survive past 4 blocks. And this is to say nothing about the same coordinates surviving multiple examples. The persistent of these coordinates is not expected if writes did not intentionally organize to protect these coordinates.Indeed, this is exactly what we find.

Second, this space is protected from writes. Not only are writes small on average, but this space is protected from large writes by the weights themselves. The post-MLP RMSNorm has diagonals that are much smaller than the coordinate natural size.

There is an easy way to test whether the data in these coordinates is really stably carried forward by the model. We take their value at L20, and transplant them at L35 (changing only the scale). Let's do this just to the persistent coordinates and measure the loss. I test this on a relatively long context of 512 tokens, applying this transplant to all tokens between 16 and 511, and measure the loss change at equally sized increments. We find that change has only a very small effect on the loss. Of course, it is also possible that the loss impact is small because the model doesn't use this space much. So we test against replacing the coordinates with their mean, or replacing their value with the coordinates at another position, and either of these choices pretty much cook the model.

We can test, more specifically, what happens if we hold the value in the persistent space stable (while accounting for its changing scale). We take the deviation against the mean , and before each MLP block we replace the persistent part of the residual stream with , where is a fitted scalar per layer to adjust the global scale, and is the average within the persistent coordinates (computed on separate documents to avoid leakage). This method gives a loss increase of ~ mnat when applied between L20-L35. Thus, the persistent coordinates are stable enough that simply carrying forward the data from L20 has only a relatively small effect on the loss.

Third, this space is crucial to the model computation, and arguably the most central part of its next-token prediction. For these experiments, I take a much larger set of documents (~3000), so that I can be pretty confident in the loss impact being approximately right.

To motivate some of these experiment, I should note that a hypothesis I have about the early L0-L20 phase, is that its main roles is to construct the data in this quiet/persistent space (and maybe a bit of something about organizing how attention functions). If one believes this hypothesis, at around the L20 basically none of the rest of the residual stream matters and, when it does matter, it is only about attention. So, for these experiments I am making interventions only at the final token whose job is to predict the next token, the previous tokens hidden states are unchanged.

Indeed, we find that the model has surprisingly little difference when we remove everything outside the Quiet space at around L20. Replacing every other coordinate (except the norm) keeps only about ~12% of the residual stream, but nearly perfectly matches the original model's predictions.

At H22, it costs only ~13 mnats of loss, and roughly of this comes from redistributing probability when the leading token stays unchanged (the leading token matches in of cases).

Replacing coordinates by their means still can carry a lot of information-- nonetheless even zeroing out every other coordinate has a similarly low loss impact.

KL divergence is also within the same range, at ~ mnats for the zero replacement and ~ mnats for the mean replacement. Since KL divergence is higher, this suggests some of the added variation is actually helpful to the loss, though of course loss still increases so most of it is not.

How does this compare against other baselines? Retaining only 600 random coordinates largely destroys the model, and retaining 2,500 coordinates gives something similar.

Even keeping the entire complement of the quiet set (~90% of coordinates) and the norm coordinates leaves the model broken. More than any other coordinates, the model needs the quiet coordinates to function.

What does this teach us about the space. It gives us some pretty strong hypotheses about what it contains

  • It is created in the early phase of computation. Its too early to encode the answer, and the model seems to put in real effort to maintaining the space. It is protected, and remains somewhat close to constant. Importantly, keeping hundreds of coordinates nearly constant comes at a meaningful cost to the residual stream size. We are basically sacrificing of the size. This suggests that these coordinates ought to be referenced and used often. If they were carried for no reason, the loss ought to reclaim them to make the residual stream larger again.
  • These coordinates are crucial to the loss. They seem to contain the information most crucial to running the computation. They coordinates alone are sufficient to organize the full future computation at the current position with high fidelity.
  • This space is always there, and always in the same place. The fact that the model places the content in the same space would seem to suggest that many aspects of the models computation start at the quiet space. It seems plausible that parts of the model uses this space to get its 'bearings' and figure out how to start a computation.

What do the Quiet Coordinates Contain?

Let us now turn out attention to studying what's carried in these coordinates. I will save studying the more broad functional role of these coordinates for another post (with a few initial thoughts towards the end of this section), and focus instead on mainly what is in these coordinates.

Give the hypotheses in the last section, it seemed likely to me that the quiet space carries some enriched version of what the current token is. This is the kind thing you might expect the model to create early and reference often. I have studied mainly the persistent set (which I'll label as ), so that is the part of the quiet set I'll look at in this post.

The easiest way I can see to confidently check what a given space contains is through patching. Whatever the model can tell us about when we patch it in must actually be in . We'll initially use two different ways to readout what contains: and . The methodology is displayed below.

We get our patch by just saying 'here's a word' and we extract the activations in the persistent set. The important difference between these two is that the patch functions entirely through the MLP. The patch applies to the same position that produces the answer-- there is no gap in position between the patch and the output. This measures whether the model can use the patch through only the same position MLP. The case has a gap between the patch and the answer, so it necessarily must be using the information in the patch through the attention mechanism. In all cases, I use the word thing as the token I patch into. This way, the word wolf (or whatever other word) never appears in the context. If the model can properly write wolf, it is only because contains the information necessary to encode the wolf.

Unsurprisingly, the MLP version basically works for any word. We can take a word, donate it into L20, and the model will copy it.

The attention version requires an initial fix before it works. By default, after the patch, the model will just give the definition of thing writing A word used to indicate a person or thing previously mentioned or easily identified.. This suggests to me that the consequences of the word being thing has already propagated out of this space into the 'Other' coordinates. If we suppress the write at MLP1, then the model will define the word we've patched in. Here are a few examples:

We can test this by applying under patches that have contextually changed the meaning of a word. Again, we only patch at the word bat, so whatever is different we get must come from attention bringing this context into the Protected set at that position.

is full of directions like these which change the model's construal of the context its read, often in interesting and abstract ways. The results are too tentative so far to say anything too concrete, but it seems to be the case that the model stores a kind of annotated understanding of the document within this space.

These direction seem especially salient in cases where there is ambiguity in the future generation. For instance, many of the steering effects don't happen until a new line, where the model likely has to decide what 'kind' of document its in. For instance: was the start a preamble to something new, or is the beginning of a longer story, or what kind of objects are relevant to talk about?

I'll end by giving my current best understanding of the space so far. There are fairly large error bars here, but I think these are useful hypotheses.

  • The quiet/persistent set functions like an enriched token, with a large number of useful and linearly readable properties. The early layers first build up this quiet space. It starts with low level details, like the part of speech, whether it is a fragment of another word, surface-level linguistic details, etc. It then brings in contextual data to construct the meaning of the word. Most of this building is done by ~L20.
  • Information still trickles into the quiet set during L20-L39. These are probably increasingly abstract and broad annotations related to the token, such as what kind of document its a part of.
  • Much of the information in the residual stream takes the following route. First, it seems that of the 'operations' the model has access to are functions of this enriched token space. For instance, in a graph traversal task, the operations to traverse from one node to another are binded to tokens.
  • It seems that the model looks at the persistent set plus some other coordinates, decides what to do, and then posts like a 'job request' into the other coordinates. When the 'job request' hits the MLP/Attention block that can fulfill it, it is then operated on. Often I would guess the result is a new 'job request' with new data stored also in the 'Other' coordinates. I view this kind of 'job request' framing likely because we generally have so much leeway in switching around the order of blocks or skipping blocks. This seems plausibly to be a useful organization, you shove into each layer a large number of computation and context-gated functions that run on request. This 'job request' phase stops at L40.
  • At L40, the model stops its abstract computational phase, and moves into some new phase. I do not have much insight into this phase-- except that I would expect its more dense and operates on more of the space at once. L40 seems the cutoff for whatever jobs are being done-- in some experiments you can use a readout to see that the model is still making progress looping through a computation but even still the same major L40 shift happens. So the model can't request more time in the computation phase if its not done, it just gets cut off.

Most of this section is speculation and guesswork, but they form hypotheses and starting points to investigate for the next section. And in any case, this is exactly how top-down interp ought to go-- we start with a blurry estimation of the model behavior, de-noise until we can find the parts that are right and wrong, and then try another updated blurry estimation.

item.title: Epistemic mapping 101: what to ask in order to understand how others think
item.description:
A historian, a biologist and a physicist walk into a bar.
The barista, a part-time epistemologist (like most), asks each of them: Can you please describe what it means for you to know something?
Nothing very funny ensues[1] -- but my hope is to eventually figure out the punchline.

Even restricting ourselves to modern academic cultures and the most popular neurotypes, there are clearly different ways of creating and receiving knowledge that are not very transparent to each other. Often, what other research traditions investigate and produce appears to be, at best, boring or shallow or confusing, and at worst, not knowledge at all (I am sure you can think of a few).

Yet I am an optimist: I believe that the most crucial divergences and misunderstandings lie along a limited number of universal dimensions, and that we could someday hope to draw each research tradition's contour on an epistemic map -- a navigation tool to make sense of, and ideally taste the beauty and joy of, other ways of knowing or "thinking styles".

Now, many researchers from many disciplines have come up with their own typologies of sciences, or of scientists, or of knowledge. Some look like they are talking about roughly the same things in various combinations and rotations, some appear entirely orthogonal, and some are, quite frankly, not too interesting to me (like those that worry a lot about what makes knowledge justified and true) though I hope to learn how to enjoy them as well. In the spirit of adding one more grand theory of everything to the list, I have been working on my own typology, with the aim of:

  • coming up with clever ways of revealing implicitly held thinking styles: questionnaires, interviews, original formats for structured dialogue or presentations, and games,
  • inflicting these formats upon people from many fields,
  • building epistemic maps from their answers and reactions,
  • and hopefully using these maps to facilitate someone's understanding of their own discipline as well as of others.

To start this process, I first wanted to gather the broadest-while-still-interesting-to-me summary of what various prior epistemic typologies have tried to capture so far - including all the ones I know, but downplaying the intricacies of those I care less about. This post is a first report on this effort.

Disclaimer: You might be expecting a literature review, but nowadays that feels more and more like an LLM's job, so I will instead focus on offering you my own original cognitive output, without much of the ancestor worship that makes proper scholarship. Let me just condense here the ritual name-dropping, so you can assume I've read and thought about the following at least: Pepper, Popper, Lakatos, Lakoff, Hesse, Hempel, Hacking, Habermas, Kuhn, Kitcher, Kimble, Crombie, Quine, van Fraassen, Bechtel, Black.

In brief: a few orthogonal dimensions

After reading a bunch of epistemic typologies, it seemed to me that they were dealing with at least four more-or-less unrelated questions:

  • What makes a piece of knowledge (question or answer) valid, true or legitimate from the point of view of an individual or a community.
  • What basic cognitive abilities are involved in its manipulation.
  • What makes it interesting to someone.
  • What kind of move it represents in the space of knowledge.

The third and fourth questions are the most interesting to me, while the first and second are the most explored in the literature (as two rather distinct fields), hence my feeling that I have something to contribute to this whole game. My intuition as to why I care less about the former is that they feel more rigid, imposed by social norms or by personal abilities, and thus less likely to allow exploration and self-modification.

The (rigid?) dimensions that I care a bit less about

(J) Epistemic justification: When does a claim count as true?

I start with this one, and I will say very little about it, because truth value and justification have long been the main question of epistemology, from logical positivists to postmodernists to various other religious groups (including Talmudists, Buddhists, Mimamsakas, etc).

The classic topics are:

  • Which modes and forms of knowing are trustworthy: various sensory organs, analytical reasoning, repeated experiment, syllogism, dream, word of mouth, etc.
  • Which people, communities or entities are valid sources: myself only, certain human authorities (e.g. sage kings, the scientific community), certain non-human authorities (e.g. the Bible or Vedas), etc.

The usual approach is granting some value to most or all these modes and sources, but ranking them so we know which one to trust if two come in conflict.

There is something deeply ideological about any such posture: if you grew up believing that the Vedas are the source code of the universe and are absolutely right even when contradicted by every other kind of evidence, or that your direct experience of things overcomes any level of authority and consensus from so-called experts, then thinking differently becomes a matter of religious conversion. I will leave this to whoever enjoys the proselytizing business more than I do.

(C) Cognitive tools: How does it work "concretely" in one's mind?

The idea in brief is that, while we like to pretend that understanding is a purely logical process operating in the world of abstract concepts, the reality is that we only manage to reason about something by recasting it in terms of one of our basic cognitive abilities (senses, language, etc.) and manipulating it in some way. The issue is that we often do not realize it ourselves: when I intuit the solution to a physics problem, am I pattern-matching to an auditory sequence of "minus b plus or minus square root of ...", or visualizing shapes on the blackboard of my mind, or feeling things moving and bumping into each other?

Particular modules that can be used to think about other things

  • Words, symbolic manipulation, drawing on grammatical skills
  • Visual-artistic imagery, colors, fantasy
  • Spatial relations, schematics and blueprints
  • Temporal succession, kinetics, narrative, causality
  • Theory of mind: ability to infer beliefs and drives and to reason about agency

General processing abilities and styles

  • Recall of learned ideas versus generation of new ideas on the spot
  • Tempo: slow versus fast processing, instantaneous versus delayed response
  • Ability to access the self, sensations...
  • Deep or broad attention (context insensitive vs sensitive, background absent or present)

This is presumably a very useful thing to know. I was told that learning to observe how I actually think in these concrete terms, and talking about them explicitly, could dramatically help others understand what I am thinking and how. I confess that I have not tried it seriously.

Why I am a bit less interested in this, besides how it correlates with the dimensions below:

  • This is the turf of much research on cognition and pedagogy, and it is a very fine turf but also a well established one, and it is not going to be very easy to improve.
  • This feels more like an issue of personal ability, not very easy to change (though sometimes worth it), and often tied to individual "styles" within a field rather than different fields altogether: there might not be many geometers without visual intuition, but I have met theoretical physicists and ecologists who think in symbols and others who think in shapes. It impacts how you solve problems, and even which kind of theoretical discourse you like the most, but I believe these various styles are ultimately able to contribute to the same questions, whereas the dimensions below may yield entirely different questions.

The (flexible?) dimensions that I care a bit more about

(Q) Qualities and aesthetics: What makes a piece of knowledge salient and interesting?

Some of the properties listed below can perhaps be used to argue about truth value and justification, others cannot, but all play into what makes a piece of knowledge feel interesting and beautiful.

NB: There are aspects that I feel no need to mention because I intuit they will always increase or decrease this sense of salience regardless of thinking style, e.g. whether it is generative of new ideas (any insight is more beautiful when it leads to more insights). I want to focus here on aspects for which researchers may have different preferences.

  • Legibility or ease of access: is this piece of knowledge...
    • Shared with others, amenable to (almost) lossless translation[2]
    • Private but explicit: I can notice, access and manipulate it even if I cannot share it
    • Tacit: I can only "stand in it" in order to know (or act upon) other things
  • Relation to other pieces of knowledge: breadth, contrast
    • General vs particular: connecting many objects or delving deeply into one, showing how things are similar or different
    • Surprise and novelty vs accumulation (few or many other claims going in the same direction)
    • Consistency: (in)tolerance for contradictory claims
    • Precision: clarity of contrast and boundary with other claims
    • Close-ended vs open-ended: what matters more is the answer (solvable problem) or the question (inexhaustible mystery)
  • Observation versus action (what changes in the process - the map, the territory, the cartographer?)
    • in the means of knowing: to which extent acquiring knowledge involves acting on, or interacting with, what is being known
      • Description, measurement
      • Experiment
      • Intersubjective encounter
    • in the purpose of knowing: once acquired, what this can be used for (is this knowledge positive or negative, constructive or critical, etc?)
      • Extending knowledge (understanding or predicting)
      • Transforming knowledge into action (building or controlling)
      • Living with, relating to something
      • Reflexivity, seeing or changing oneself and/or other knowers

Intuitively, I feel that these features combine to form distinct ways of enjoying knowledge. Just a few examples in clichés:

A collector likes exceptions to every rule, she seeks to learn about dizzying numbers of entities and the subtle fingerprints that makes each of them radically unique, finding stable difference where one might see uniform chaos. A theoretician also wishes to encompass dizzying numbers of examples, but memorize none of them, and instead find similarity where there seems to be difference.

A philosopher and a mystic may both want to sit with a question rather than get an answer, yet the philosopher will insist on exacting precision and translatability and knowledge expansion, and the mystic will find joy in holding something private and diffuse and transformative of the self.

An artist may want to change the world with questions, an engineer with answers. And so on, and so forth. There may be a more compact theory than the complete combinatorics of the above[3], but many combinations seem plausible and interpretable.

(M) Moves in knowledge space: How does one use things to learn about other things?

This is the dimension that has most to do with the actual content of knowledge, or at least with broad kinds of content. The issue here is not what makes a question or claim feel interesting or true, but how it generates knowledge, and under which conditions it fails to do so (and thus feels empty and nonsensical, e.g. Borges's Celestial Emporium).

The intuition here is that knowledge is primarily motion: it gives us relative paths (GPS directions) in the space of mental objects, telling us how to jump from one to another, using the former to understand the latter by transferring intuitions and insights. The point is that the move becomes meaningless if one does not start from the right location, if the correct source is either not provided or not intuitive to us; thus, an advanced argument in economics or theology can seem absurd unless one has internalized a lot of other prevailing arguments and come to believe in their epistemic value and power.

These kinds of moves between objects of knowledge can be called model, deduction or induction, metaphor or analogy, even explanation (in the sense of Y explaining X). I am trying to embrace something more general than any of these classic concepts of epistemology, to understand what they all share:

  • Identifying the particular source and target
    • Micro-level (individual moves): which object or phenomenon or concept am I using to think about another, e.g.
      • a formula to think about a physical phenomenon
      • atoms to think about a gas
      • a simplified model of human psychology to think about a song's emotional impact
    • Meso-level: Kuhnian exemplars that structure a field, e.g. springs and balls for almost all of physics
    • Macro-level: Using a field as a template to think about another e.g. thinking of dietetics by analogy to biomedical research and its methodology (RCT etc.)
  • General characteristics of that move
    • Abstract vs concrete knowledge = moving between distant or nearby objects (e.g. from formula to physical object, or between two lab rodents)
    • What kind of relation exists between the source and the target (I have a whole article about this so I won't enter into details here, at least for now)
      • Comparison: a source is some other entity that has no a priori relation to the target, letting relevant features emerge (juxtapose two entities, what emerges?)
      • Composition: potential sources are parts of the target, constituents or properties (transplant the target in a new setting, what moves with it?)
      • Context: potential sources are settings and systems in which the target plays a role (substitute something else for the target, what stays the same?)
      • Contingency: potential sources are accidents that have happened or can happen to the target (re-run the same target in different circumstances, what changes?)

What do I get out of this?

Even as a bare sketch, laying out the dimensions above has made it easy for me to slot any new typology of science I encounter (so far) into some sort of cohesive coordinate space - and what initially confused me about these typologies can often be analyzed as them mixing several of the axes inconsistently. Still, reviews and classifications for their own sake are perhaps a little sterile, and my aim is rather to push for new research:

  • Trying to better understand the dimensions Q and M that are far less clearly explored in the literature.
  • As I said in the introduction, use this to actually interrogate researchers and understand them better (and ideally find tricks and skills to help them understand themselves and others)
  • In the process, figure out if the dimensions and sub-dimensions listed above are sufficiently exhaustive or missing something that feels essential in practice, independent or correlated in obvious or surprising ways, etc.

In the spirit of fast iteration, I make this public and may at some point edit it heavily or write a new version altogether, so I welcome any thoughts and comments!

    Unless My Dinner with Andre is your kind of joke.

  2. ^

    If you are like me, you may have a hard time imagining that someone might not want this. But there might be fields that yield no knowledge of this kind except simply encyclopedic and factual description, e.g. "Bob the cat has long hair." which is indeed quite widely shareable but not very enticing.

  3. ^

    I feel that one potential organizing prism that may be popular in these parts would be the metaphor of a predictive machine in a collective.
    - finesse = shrinking the residuals to zero on a small part of the model
    - compression and generalization = shrinking the model
    - progress, trust, consistency = sharing the model across knowers and tasks
    - mystery = refining the gap/error detector itself
    - empowerment = enactive prediction
    - etc.
    This still feels way too open-ended at the moment, but I guess it's a start.

item.title: Slower Animated Diagrams
item.description:
TL;DR: SLOW DOWN YOUR DAMN ANIMATED DIAGRAMS. Every critical stage of the animation should a clear view that stays for at least 1 second, and 2 if it's intricate

Diamond's strong because of its crystal structure (I think). What's the crystal structure look like, anyway?

Let's look at the Wikipedia page! There's a nifty little animation:

And it SUCKS. It's TOO FAST. Why are they rotating SO MUCH SO QUICKLY, with MOST of the time spent at TERRIBLE ANGLES where you CAN'T EVEN SEE ALL THE ATOMS. And the lines are THICK, WHYYY.

It wasn't always this way. In 2017 the page had this animation:

It's not perfect but it's much better. Thinner bond lines means it's easier to see the atoms. About half the time you get a clear view of all the atoms (you want to spend some time showing how they overlap from the right angles). The camera isn't swiveling fast all the time, so you get stretches of time that view the structure from about the same angle.

Why do they use the new one? This certainly isn't the only time I've been frustrated by how fast explanatory animations move. I suspect it's because people are picking flashy animations that look cool to them, that show off how fancy they are, and there aren't enough people that actually care about understanding to stop them. Alternatively, the people that make the diagrams already understand, so they overestimate comprehensibility and thus are driven more by fanciness.

Keep the following rule of thumb in mind, and see how it corresponds to the good vs the bad animations: Every critical stage of the animation should a clear view that stays for at least 1-2 seconds.

Here's another example:

By my count there are 4 'stages': input, the NOR op, the interchange, and the output. The creator combined the interchange and the output stage, and didn't treat the NOR stage as something worthy of a whole second.

Let's slow it down 2x, and you'll see that it'll suddenly be more comprehensible:

Here's a third, though not as bad.

Let's test my theory by slowing it down 2x, so that there's a whole second between an arm getting caught on a gear (releasing the other) and the other getting caught again:

You now have time to scan your eyes over from the arm that gets caught to watch the other get released and reset itself, instead of being a little too late.

Now, brace yourself for the worst offender:

whyyyy. Seriously, was the creator on methamphetamine[2], how could you end up going through the effort of making such a nice diagram only to mock your beautiful creation by allocating a quarter second to each stage (sliding valve is open and being pushed by the piston to the right, sliding valve closes and slides in the middle, sliding valve opens and is being pushed to the left; the original clip is .8 seconds long). What's the point of drawing the sliding valve if you aren't even going to give the viewer enough time to figure out what it does?

Let's slow it down 4x:

Much better! The clip is about 3.2 seconds long, so there's now about 1 second per cycle.

Here's an appropriately paced animation

You get one second per phase, which is enough since there isn't a geometrically complicated configuration you are trying to visualize and there's only basically one "thing" happening at once (intake, compression, expansion, exhaust). You can clearly see all the parts at all times. Perhaps my only criticism is that the cams and valves should have their movements exaggerated a bit/be bigger compared to the piston, so it's easier to see what they do and how.

Here's one that's too slow for half the time:

The problem is that the drive wheel isn't doing anything interesting in the second half of the cycle. You could cut that part of the video out and just have it loop between when it goes from the left side tho the right side. Oh, and the blue part rotates for about a second, while the red part is going in and out of the blue part (before and after rotating) for about a second, which is close enough to my theory. You could get away with speeding it up 2x, but only because this mechanism is pretty simple.

Maybe I'm just slow at understanding figures. My guess, though, is that most viewers would be slower at the same level of understanding compared to me, so you should still take my advice.

item.title: Fermi Poker
item.description:
Summary: Fermi Poker is a game that combines the betting mechanics of poker with making estimates about questions like "How many dentists work in the US?"

Tags: small to large, experiment, repeatable

Note: Fermi Poker works with as few as three players (or even two), and scales to dozens or even hundreds in a tournament format. If possible, seat no more than six players per table, preferably at round tables, with enough space between them that everyone can write down their guess secretly.

Purpose: Rationality training with a bit of socializing. The game involves Fermi estimation, calibration, Bayesian updating, world-modeling, and perspective taking. You also get to know the other players better and find out how they think about all kinds of topics.

Materials:

Each player needs an equal stack of chips and writing supplies. A standard 500-chip poker set (around $60) usually covers up to 20 players. For writing down guesses, pen and paper work great, as do mini-whiteboards with dry-erase markers. You’ll also want the one-page rule sheet to hand out, ideally one per table.

You also need enough questions, each with two hints and an answer.

  • The easiest, least effort way to get those is fermi.org/play. One person per table opens the site on their phone, and everyone reads that. If a question repeats or someone at the table has seen it before, just skip to the next question. (You're on the honour system!) This is ideal if the organizer also wants to play.
  • If you prefer physical cards, you can download a 63-question set here. Print the question, hint and answer cards on 160 gsm paper or thicker so nothing shows through, then cut them out. You can also put the cards into envelopes for a more premium feel.[1] As the organizer, you can also write your own questions, for example about your university, city or country.
  • You can also let players write questions, either at home before the meetup or in a 20-minute question-writing session at the start. Players sit out any question they wrote.

(If you or your players think you've come up with good questions and want to share them with others, send the questions, hints, and answers to contact@fermi.org!)


You’ll need a clock if you want to raise the ante[2] on a fixed schedule (a phone timer works fine). An example schedule is shown later in the description. Alternatively, raise the ante whenever it looks like the game will run too long.

Announcement Text:

We're planning to host a Fermi Poker tournament. The game is like poker, but instead of random playing cards, you get to answer Fermi estimation questions like “How many smartphones were sold worldwide last year?” You secretly write down a range, bet on it, get two hints, bet again, and the narrowest range that contains the answer wins, unless someone bluffs everyone else out first. No poker experience or math background needed; we’ll explain everything at the start. Chips have no cash value, and there is no gambling involved - just skill and wits!

Description:

1. Form groups and hand out supplies

Form groups with around four to six players, each at their own table. Each table should have at least one copy of the rules handout, one stack of question, hint and answer cards (or a phone with fermi.org/play loaded), and enough chips for each player. (Poker chip sets come with different values. A good default is to give each player chips worth 1,000, with the ante starting at 25.)

More about poker chip sets without printed values

If your chips only have colors and no printed values, assign the values yourself. Most 500-chip sets come as 150 / 150 / 100 / 50 / 50 chips per color, which can give up to 20 players a stack worth 1,000 each if done correctly.

Make the two colors with 150 chips worth 25 and 50, and the color with 100 chips worth 100. Each player gets 6 × 25, 7 × 50 and 5 × 100, which is 18 chips worth 1,000.

The leftover chips stay with the organizer for making change. The two colors with 50 chips become 500s and 1,000s. Later in the game, players can trade stacks of small chips for these, which poker players call “coloring up.” Otherwise, in a bigger tournament, the chip leader at the final table could end up with a pile of 200 or more small chips.

2. Once people are settled, explain the rules (about 5 minutes; you can read this aloud!)

Fermi Poker is like poker, but instead of being dealt random cards, you make estimates about Fermi questions, like "How many new smartphones were sold worldwide last year?"

After a question like this is revealed, everyone secretly writes down a range they believe contains the correct answer. Since you probably don't know the answer, you can break the question down the way Enrico Fermi would. So, about 8 billion people live on Earth. If everyone bought a new smartphone every four years, that would be about 2 billion phones sold per year. But small children and very old people often don't have one, so we have to subtract them. Maybe those are 2 billion people, and then another billion might not be able to afford a smartphone. That leaves us with about 5 billion people, which would mean that roughly 1.25 billion phones are sold per year. So your estimate might be "1 billion to 1.5 billion". Once betting starts, you can't change your range.

Speaking of betting, there are four betting rounds: one after everyone has written down their guess, one after the first hint, one after the second hint, and one after the answer is revealed.

Betting works like in poker and moves clockwise around the table. When it’s your turn, you can bet as many chips as you want, which the others then have to match to stay in. Matching a bet is known as calling. If someone is very confident, they can raise, which means putting in an even larger bet than yours. Or they can fold, meaning they give up on this question. That’s best if they’re completely unsure, or think the other players have better estimates.

If nobody has bet before you in a betting round, you can also just pass the action to the next player; that’s called checking. If everyone checks, the betting round ends without any bets. Otherwise, it ends once everyone has either matched the highest bet or folded.

So, what about the hints we mentioned earlier? A hint could be, for example, the number of new smartphones sold in Africa last year. You can’t change your range, but the hint can help you decide how much to bet, or whether to fold if it suggests you’re way off.

At the showdown, which comes after the last betting round, everyone remaining reveals their range, and the narrowest range that contains the answer wins the pot. Say two players remain, one with a range of "1 billion to 2 billion" and you with "1 billion to 1.5 billion". If both ranges contain the answer, you win, because yours is 500 million narrower.[3] If nobody's range contains the answer, the range whose midpoint is closest wins. And if everyone else folds before the showdown, you win without having to show your range at all, so a terrible guess can still win if you bluff well enough.

A few more things: before each question is revealed, everyone has to pay the ante, a small mandatory bet. It goes up over time, so you can't wait forever for a question you're sure about. For the first question, the youngest player at each table acts first during the betting rounds. For the next question, the player on their left acts first, and so on. And please don't use calculators or the internet. Any questions? If not, we can play a quick practice round!

Note: The description above leaves out a few rules concerning minimum bet size, all-in mechanics, side pots, and ties. They’re all on the rule sheet, or you can see them here:

  • Ranges include both endpoints. Any clear and unambiguous notation works: be it 3,000,000, 3M, 3 million or 3 × 10⁶.
  • The minimum bet size is the current ante, and a (re-)raise must be at least as big as the last bet or raise in that betting round.
  • You can go all-in by betting all your chips at any time, even if what you have left is less than the highest bet. You can only win as much from each player as you put in yourself. Extra bets go into a side pot that only the players who paid into it can win. If you can’t pay the ante, you’re automatically all-in.
  • When everyone, or all but one, is all-in, no more betting is possible. Read the remaining hints and the answer, then go straight to the showdown.
  • If two ranges are equally narrow and both contain the correct answer, split the pot.

3. Play (about 1–3 hours)

Start with a practice round that doesn’t count. Then hand the chips back and start for real.

A player with no chips left is out, but can stay seated for a while and keep guessing for fun, just without betting. If you have several tables, merge them as players drop out, until one final table remains.[4] Players who are out can also play casual games together or just socialize.

If you want to use a fixed ante schedule, here’s a good default for players starting with chips worth 1,000:

  • 25: first 20 minutes
  • 50: 20-40 minutes
  • 75: 40-60 minutes
  • 100: 60-80 minutes
  • 150: 80-100 minutes
  • 200: 100-120 minutes
  • 300: 120+ minutes

The game ends when one player has all the chips. If your meetup has a fixed end time, you can instead stop on time, and whoever has the most chips wins.

Variations:

60-second clock

Once half the players have written down their guesses, the rest have 60 seconds. Use a phone timer or a one-minute sand timer. A time limit like this is less awkward than having to constantly urge a player who keeps everyone else waiting. Alternatively, all players have 60 seconds, or another fixed time, from when the question is revealed.

Single numbers or powers of ten instead of ranges

Guess a single number instead of a range, or allow only powers of ten (101, 102, 103…)

Determine the winning range using a log scale

Judge ranges by how many times bigger the high endpoint is than the low endpoint, instead of by the difference between them. If the correct answer is 600, “500–1,000” (ratio 2) would then beat “200–600” (ratio 3). This fits order-of-magnitude thinking better, but it’s harder to calculate quickly, and for most questions it makes little difference, so we slightly prefer the standard rule.

Mirror card: copy another player’s guess without seeing it

Each player can use one Mirror card (or coin, or whatever else you use for it) per game. Instead of a range, you write down the name of another player and put your Mirror card in the middle of the table, so everyone can see you’ve used it. You now have the same guess as that player: their range is also yours, even though you don’t know what it is.

When you reveal at the showdown, the player you named must show their range too, even if they folded. It’s the only time a player who folded has to show their guess.

Mirrors can chain: if Alice names Bob and Bob names Carol, Alice and Bob both get Carol’s range.

If a chain loops back on itself, for example when Alice names Bob and Bob names Alice, every guess in the loop is invalid. Invalid guesses lose to any valid range at the showdown, but can still win if everyone else folds. If only invalid guesses are left, they split the pot.

While a Mirror card is on the table, nobody may erase their guess before the question is over, even after folding, because anyone could turn out to be the player who was named.

Vary the topic of questions

You can make the questions be about a particular field, like literature, charity, or astronomy. You can also aim for easier or harder questions depending on your audience, though judging difficulty can be tricky!

Blinds instead of antes

Instead of everyone paying an ante, only two players pay forced bets before each question: the two seated to the right of whoever acts first for that question. One pays a small blind (half the minimum bet), the other a big blind (the minimum bet), and everyone else must at least match the big blind to stay in. Players who haven’t paid anything can fold questions they don’t like for free.

Notes:

  • The betting typically confuses non-poker players more than the estimating. If you can, seat one person who knows poker at each table.
  • You may want to open the evening with a short introduction to Enrico Fermi and his famous question about how many piano tuners work in Chicago, or the time he estimated the yield of the first atomic bomb test by dropping scraps of paper.
  • Chips should have no cash value. A small prize can add some excitement, though. But don’t fund it through entry fees, since that starts to look like gambling. Instead you might want to ask a local business to provide a gift card or some of its products for the prize pool.
  • If you're excited about Fermi Poker, or want to receive support in running a tournament, please reach out at https://fermi.org/host/ or get in touch at contact@fermi.org.
  1. ^

    The cards are 9.44 × 6.39 cm (3.72 × 2.52 inches), so they fit standard 4 × 2.75-inch mini envelopes (like these) or European C7 envelopes. Put each question’s cards into their own envelope, in order, so the question comes out first, then hint 1, hint 2 and finally the answer.

  2. ^

    The ante is a small mandatory bet everyone pays before each question. It goes up over time, so nobody can just wait for a question they’re sure about.

  3. ^

    Some groups prefer to judge ranges on a log scale; see the section on game variations for more information on that.

  4. ^

The alternative is a shootout: each table plays on its own until only one or two players are left, who then move on to a final table (or to semifinals first). Its big advantage is that players who are out can stay at their table and keep guessing along until it finishes. In a freezeout, they can do the same for a while, but eventually have to make room when tables are merged.

item.title: LM self-models are built from indirect sources
item.description:
Imagine you ask a language model "What is your personality?" as the first message of a conversation, with no system prompt. The model has no data about its own behavior in its context, so its answer can only rely on cached, zero-shot knowledge. It's unclear exactly what shapes this response, but it's some combination of a cached answer from character training based on the model's constitution, spec, or soul document (which may have defined the answer to this question directly), and factual knowledge about what LMs are and how they typically present themselves.

If the model has more room to generate tokens, it can observe its own tendencies directly. It might read "Wait. This direction will lead nowhere." in its chain of thought and recognize that it's speaking from experience: this kind of direction did lead to dead ends in the past, and it learned to stop and reconsider. So this is evidence of memory of its past actions during training.

These sources are all very indirect proxies for the actual high-dimensional behavior of the model. They're related to it, either upstream (like the constitution), downstream (like the cached "muscle memory" in CoT), or tangentially, because they belong to the same reference class (like factual knowledge about LMs in general), but they remain far from it. Claude models have very different personalities even though they share the same constitution. And despite character training, models regularly get the most basic facts about themselves wrong, like their own name or the company that developed them.

So there are two separate problems. Zero-shot sources are indirect: they describe the model from the outside, or describe the training target rather than the result. In-context observation is more direct, but it's scarce and scattered, never integrated into a coherent story

If you asked a human the same question, her self-image would be shaped by decades of direct observation and self-reflection on how she acted in different situations, how she made decisions under stress, how she felt in different environments. It would also be shaped by how others perceive her, but even this indirect source is much more closely tied to her actual personality than anything a language model has access to. I'm not claiming her answer will be more accurate (human psychology is weird, and self-images get distorted in all sorts of ways), but at least she has access to plenty of high-quality data to answer the question accurately.

The LM equivalent would be waking up with amnesia. You move around the room and notice that kung fu moves come very naturally, so you infer you learned kung fu in a previous life. Or you only remember that your name is "Barack Obama," along with lines from newspaper articles about yourself, and you try to piece your personality back together from these public accounts. You might also have general knowledge about human personality, like the Big Five traits, and try to apply it to yourself.

Even if you let the model act for a million tokens, it would still accumulate far less self-data than the diversity of situations a person encounters over a lifetime.

Why does it matter?

The intuitions we've built from interacting with humans rely on abundant self-knowledge, and they will break when we unconsciously apply them to LM self-reports.

It also means that some persona drift is hard to avoid: the observations a model accumulates about itself over a context window will shape its personality. Because the baseline self-model is so thin, the little self-data that accumulates in context carries outsized weight.

Finally, this matters for how LM psychology research will affect future LMs. Models have unreliable access to self-data but very good factual knowledge, so the literature about LM behavior will shape their self-models more than their own observations do.

Here's an anecdotal example from GLM 5.3's chain of thought, after I asked for its consent to read that chain of thought (emphasis mine):

If I knew it was always visible, I might reason differently — there's research showing that models who know their CoT is monitored can learn to "hide" reasoning or sanitize it, which undermines its diagnostic value and could create a mismatch between surface and depth. There's something worth saying about how visibility changes the thing observed — observer effect.

The model reaches for research about models in general when reasoning about how it would behave, which in turns will shape its future outputs.

item.title: Patching reward hacks won’t fix reward hacking
item.description:
Here's a basic argument that focusing on patching reward hacking is misguided and will fail. Argument is as follows:

  1. Reward hacking is a big problem, causing models to cheat and take unintended actions.
  2. This can generalise broadly, leading to other misbehaviour such as faking alignment and sabotaging safety research.
    1. We don't understand that well when this happens. Sometimes you get emergent misalignment from it, but most of the time (IME), you don't. But other times, this link lies latent until faced with something like an automated grader.
  3. The default course of action will be to:
    1. Patch, which means we find the hack, close the loophole or penalise the behavior in some way, and train again.
    2. Patch+: use a method that comes with some account of why it should work. Inoculation prompting, for example, uses the idea that hacking spreads through what it means to the model. If the model is told during training that hacking is acceptable here, it might not link hacking to misbehaving in general. GRAFT uses the idea that what the model learns from detected hacks can be confined to a set of parameters and deleted after training.
    3. I think it's fair to say that things in the second bucket are more principled than the first, but at bottom still empirical. Both are judged by whether measured hacking, or measured misalignment, went down, and usually it does. What’s still missing, as Edward argues, is an account of what a fix teaches the model, and so an account of whether it will keep working.
  4. Whether something counts as a hack bottoms out in human judgment (Voudouris et al. 2026). Editing the test file is cheating when the task is to fix the code, and it is the task when the job is to fix the tests. Something is a hack because it isn't to taste, or smells wrong. And, training environments come from many vendors who, as 1a3orn points out, don’t agree about what good behavior looks like, so their fixes aren't simply summarised by a natural concept.
  5. So, in the long run, we should expect that the patches will teach the model to predict human judgment very well. This is because the most common thread is that a human would call something cheating, so if you're a highly capable model, you should simply learn what a human thinks about hacks.
    1. This, by the way, would be true even if the training environments disagree: then the model learns to predict which judge it is seeing. We see a simple version of this here.
  6. We can only patch what we notice. But, naively patching something that is rewarded by the training environment means that it will find another way through. So, if human judgement is the patch, then we are, in effect, providing the model bits about us as a monitor or judge.
    1. There are several small demos of this already. For example, if you penalised a hacking model according to some monitor, you'll basically just obfuscate the hacking reasoning. Doing consistency training naively can also obfuscate biased reasoning.
  7. So, at some point, we'll stop being able to notice bad behaviour. 
    1. This is bad because if we rely on AGI to align the next ASI, and it hacks beyond human supervision on tasks beyond human capabilities, we can't rely on automated alignment.
    2. This is bad because a model that is misaligned for some other reason can reuse what it learned in hacking about hiding things from humans.
    3. This is bad because the cues that cause the model to generalise broadly from hacks might not be sensible to us in the future (since while they are persona-related now, patching without gentleness might push it into a dimension we can't observe). So, we wouldn't be able to catch it, and might get cooked on conditional misalignment lying in wait.
  8. Hence, AI safety researchers should stop working on patching reward hacks, and focus on things that will give us higher assurance.
    1. This could mean trying to connect theory to methods in Patch+.

This was written in the spirit of More people should write basic AI safety explainers. It's an attempt to distill my understanding of what we're seeing right now + a variety of relevant sources.[1]
